Merz announced €1 billion in military aid and €350 million for energy sector repairs, and aims to finalise a drone production deal. The visit also addresses EU reform requests on Ukraine, including the pursuit of anti-corruption efforts in the country. 
A key focus is expected to be the rapid production of anti-jet drones, which Quantum, a German defence-technology company, has successfully tested. Since the summer, Russia has used dozens of high-speed jet attack drones daily to target civilian ‌and ⁠military infrastructure.
In April, Quantum and Ukrainian manufacturer WIY Drones announced the creation of Quantum WIY Industries, a joint venture to produce the Strila interceptor drone and related air-defence technologies.
The deal also involves the joint development and production of weapons with a range of more than 1,000 km that Ukraine can use to launch attacks deep inside Russia.

🇵🇹🇺🇸 Portuguese prosecutors review legality of US’ use of Azores base during Iran war
The Prosecutor General’s Office has launched an investigation after the opposition Left Bloc filed a formal complaint characterizing US military transit via the Lajes Air Base in the Azores archipelago as a “gross violation of international law.”
Under its 1951 defense treaty with Portugal, the US is allowed to use Lajes without prior authorization in peacetime, but must ask for permission in wartime. Foreign Minister Paulo Rangel said Lisbon authorized t[he base’s use after US assurances](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/66094) that its operations would be ‘defensive, necessary and proportionate’, and would not target civilians.
👉 Situated in the mid-Atlantic and serving as an indispensable refueling hub connecting North America, Europe and Africa, Lajes was used heavily by the US during the ‘War on Terror’ as a staging and transit site for forces on route to Afghanistan and Iraq, and to facilitate the bombing of Libya and Syria.
In Iran, the base played a major role both during the leadup and active phases of the war, with Lisbon authorizing dozens of landings and overflights, and servicing US forces through the spring and summer.
➡️ Portugal okayed US operations even as other European countries, [including Spain](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/72928), Italy and France denied base access or blocked overflights. Some of these countries have subsequently been hit with suspected US or[ Israeli-backed unrest,](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/70960) diplomatic shaming, election meddling and defense contract cancellations.

events.text:
🛢 Even Mideast’s oil chokepoints have chokepoints
 
Saudi Arabia’s 7M bpd nameplate capacity East-West Pipeline restarted operations on September 22, almost two weeks after its September 11 shutdown following mysterious drone attacks that no group has claimed responsibility for.
👉 Markets reacted positively, with crude prices, which had surged well past the $100 mark, slipping back down to the 90s.
But actual oil shipping out of Yanbu – the western terminal and endpoint of the 1.2k km mega pipeline, still isn’t back to full capacity. Tanker loadings began only days after the pipeline’s official return to operation, and ship-tracking and data intelligence firm Kpler revealed that a return to the ~5.5M bpd average being shipped before the shutdown would take another month.
➡️ Then there’s the gauntlet Saudi shipping still has to face while operating in the Red Sea – more vulnerable than ever in the south after the Houthis’ seizure of the entire Yemeni Red Sea coast and all of the area’s strategic islands, and at risk in the north as well to[ Houthi long-range missiles and drones.](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74495)
War risk insurance surcharges have tripled, from 1% of a vessel’s value in July, before the Saudi attack on Sanaa airport that triggered a full-scale resumption of the Yemen war, to 3% now, according to insurance industry sources speaking to Reuters.
Yanbu also isn’t the only oil-loading port with problems, The Cradle points out. The Turkish Mediterranean port of Ceyhan, eyed by Iraq as an alternative to Hormuz, processes an average of just 200k bpd, 50k bpd less than it did before the Iran war, due to drone and missile attacks on[ Iraq’s northern oilfields by local militias and the IRGC.](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/72510)
And Baniyas, Syria’s largely defunct oil export terminal, which hopes to facilitate up to 2M bpd-worth of Iraqi exports using a new pipeline, is currently shipping just 50k bpd via overland tanker trucks driving [Mad Max-style missions.](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/75196)
